### OPS as the Cross-Domain Monitoring Overlay

OPS is the observability and incident response domain — it receives telemetry from all other AI security domains (DATA, MODEL, INFRA, APP, GOV) and is responsible for correlating, detecting, and responding to AI-specific security events. OPS is distinct from traditional application APM in that it must detect anomalies specific to AI systems: adversarial inputs, model extraction, behavioral drift, LLM attack patterns, and AI-assisted threat acceleration.

**ABB Boundary**:
- **OPS governs**: AI security monitoring infrastructure, threat detection logic for AI-specific attack patterns, security event correlation across AI domains, incident response playbooks for AI security events, explainability and model audit logging, and continuous model behavioral monitoring.
- **INFRA governs**: The monitoring infrastructure substrate (SIEM deployment, log pipelines, compute for monitoring workloads).
- **MODEL governs**: Model artifact integrity and supply chain. MODEL produces `inference telemetry` that OPS consumes.
- **APP governs**: Application-layer AI interaction logs. APP produces `application security telemetry` that OPS consumes.
- **Boundary interfaces**: OPS receives the `Infrastructure Security Telemetry` (INFRA), `Model Inference Telemetry` (MODEL), `Application Security Telemetry` (APP), and `Data Pipeline Security Telemetry` (DATA) interfaces. OPS produces `AI Threat Intelligence` back to all domains (as detection logic and playbooks).

**Normative decision reference**: OPS monitoring strategy SHALL align with [ADR-SEC-006](../../../../../decisions/security/ADR-SEC-006-security-monitoring-strategy.md). This is a normative enterprise decision record governing monitoring architecture choices.

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-RAD-3.9.05.md#technical-controls-requiring-implementation]

### Technical Controls Requiring Implementation

SHOULD-flagged items require documented justification when not implemented.

**Principle 1 — Continuous AI Model Behavior Monitoring**:
- Behavioral monitoring SHALL be deployed for every production AI model. Monitoring SHALL cover: prediction confidence distribution, output category distribution, input feature distribution, and inference latency.
- Drift alerts SHALL be generated when any monitored distribution diverges from baseline by more than an approved threshold. Drift alerts SHALL be routed to the ML team and SecOps for joint triage.

**Principle 2 — Adversarial Input Detection**:
- Inference API telemetry SHALL be analyzed for adversarial input indicators: unusual input feature distributions, systematic perturbation patterns, high-frequency boundary queries, and coordinated input patterns from a single source.
- Alert thresholds SHALL be defined per model based on its known sensitivity profile. Static thresholds are insufficient; thresholds SHOULD incorporate rolling baseline computation.

**Principle 3 — Model Explainability and Audit**:
- Explainability output (feature importance or equivalent attribution) SHALL be generated and stored for a representative sample of high-stakes decisions, at minimum. Explanation method selection (SHAP, LIME, attention weights, or equivalent) is a model-specific implementation decision; the requirement is that explanations are produced and stored.
- Stored explanations SHALL be searchable by: user ID, session ID, decision outcome, and timestamp. Access to explanation records SHALL be governed the same as the source data.

**Principle 4 — AI Threat Intelligence Integration**:
- The SIEM SHALL be loaded with AI-specific threat intelligence including MITRE ATLAS tactics and techniques, OWASP LLM Top 10 attack patterns, and known adversarial input signatures, per [ADR-SEC-006](../../../../../decisions/security/ADR-SEC-006-security-monitoring-strategy.md).
- Threat intelligence feeds SHALL be updated on a minimum monthly cycle or when a significant new adversarial technique is published.

**Principle 5 — Incident Response for AI Systems**:
- Every production AI system SHALL have a designated AI Incident Response Playbook. Playbooks SHALL be stored in the enterprise playbook repository and SHALL be reviewed minimum annually.
- AI incident response exercises (tabletop or technical) SHALL be conducted minimum annually.
- AI incident response metrics SHALL be tracked: mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR), and mean time to recover (MTTRec) for AI security incidents.

**Principle 6 — AI-Assisted Threat Acceleration Monitoring**:
- The security operations team SHALL maintain documented detection logic for AI-generated attack artifacts: AI-crafted phishing, AI-generated malware patterns, AI-accelerated credential stuffing, and deepfake-assisted social engineering.
- Detection rules SHALL be validated with test data minimum quarterly against current AI-generation model capabilities.

**Principle 7 — Red Team and Adversarial Testing**:
- AI systems SHALL be subjected to structured adversarial testing (red team exercises) before production deployment and on a minimum annual cadence for production systems. Red team scope SHALL include all MITRE ATLAS attack categories relevant to the system's operational profile.
- Red team findings SHALL be tracked in the vulnerability management system. Critical findings SHALL be remediated before production deployment or shall require documented risk acceptance.

**Principle 8 — AI Security Metrics and Reporting**:
- AI security metrics SHALL be reported to the governance structure (see GOV ABB) on a minimum monthly basis. Required metrics include: detection rate, false positive/negative rates for AI threat detection, open vulnerability count by severity, incident count and MTTD/MTTR, and model drift event count.

### Pattern 1: Unified AI Security Telemetry Pipeline

**Purpose**: Normalize and route security-relevant events from all AI domains into a central analytics platform for correlation, detection, and investigation.

**Design**:
- **Log schema standardization**: Each AI domain adopts a shared base schema for security events (event_id, timestamp, domain, workload_id, user_id, event_type, data_classification, severity). Domain-specific fields extend this base.
- **Normalization pipeline**: A log ingestion pipeline receives raw telemetry from each domain, applies field normalization, enriches events with contextual metadata (workload classification, team ownership, active incident context), and routes to the SIEM.
- **Log tiering**: Security-relevant events (anomalies, policy violations, error patterns indicating attacks) are forwarded in near-real-time to SIEM. High-volume routine telemetry (all inference queries) uses higher-latency buffered ingestion for behavioral analysis workloads.
- **SIEM integration**: Normalized events are loaded into the SIEM in index structures that allow efficient querying by workload, model, user, and event type. Retention in the SIEM hot tier is 90 days; cold tier archival is 13 months; long-term archival for PHI-related events is 6 years.

**ADR-SEC-006 alignment**: Log sources, retention tiers, and SIEM selection SHALL comply with the enterprise monitoring strategy defined in ADR-SEC-006.

**Illustrative tooling**: Apache Kafka or AWS Kinesis for ingestion streaming; Elasticsearch/OpenSearch or Splunk for SIEM; AWS Glue or custom parser for normalization; S3 or Azure Blob with lifecycle policies for 6-year archival.

**NIST SP 800-53**: AU-2 (Audit Events), AU-11 (Audit Record Retention), SI-4 (Information System Monitoring)

### Pattern 2: AI-Specific Threat Detection Rule Set

**Purpose**: Detect adversarial attacks, model abuse, and AI-enabled threat acceleration using structured detection rules mapped to MITRE ATLAS and OWASP LLM Top 10.

**Design**:
- **Rule set structure**: Detection rules are organized in rule groups mapped to AI-specific attack taxonomy:
  - ATLAS AML.T0043 — Adversarial ML: detects systematic perturbation patterns in inference inputs via distribution analysis
  - ATLAS AML.T0020 — Model evasion: detects high-frequency boundary probing queries (many near-threshold predictions from one identity)
  - ATLAS AML.T0024 — Model extraction: detects API querying patterns consistent with querying the model with crafted inputs to reconstruct its decision boundary
  - OWASP LLM01 — Prompt injection: detects injection trigger phrases and anomalous output patterns in LLM interaction logs
  - OWASP LLM06 — Sensitive information disclosure: detects patterns in LLM output consistent with information exfiltration
  - AI-enabled threat acceleration: detects AI-generated phishing artifact patterns, credential stuffing bot patterns
- **Baseline-relative thresholds**: Detection thresholds are computed as multiples of rolling baseline rather than fixed values, adapting to normal operational volume changes.
- **Rule maintenance**: Detection rules are version-controlled and reviewed quarterly. New adversarial techniques identified from threat intelligence trigger an out-of-cycle rule review within 14 days.

**Illustrative tooling**: SIEM native rule frameworks (Splunk SPL, Elastic ESQL, Sigma rules exported to SIEM format); MITRE ATLAS Navigator for rule coverage mapping; OWASP LLM Top 10 mapping maintained in rule metadata.

**NIST SP 800-53**: SI-4 (Information System Monitoring), IR-4 (Incident Handling), RA-3 (Risk Assessment)

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-RAD-3.9.05.md#pattern-3-model-behavioral-drift-monitoring]

### Pattern 3: Model Behavioral Drift Monitoring

**Purpose**: Detect when a production model's behavior diverges from its validated state — either due to data drift, model degradation, or adversarial manipulation.

**Design**:
- **Baseline establishment**: When a model is deployed to production, the platform computes a behavioral baseline from the first N production inference requests (or from a representative validation dataset). The baseline covers: input feature distributions, prediction score distribution, output category distribution, and inference latency distribution.
- **Continuous monitoring**: After baseline establishment, monitoring jobs run on scheduled intervals (e.g., hourly for high-traffic models, daily for low-traffic forecasting models) and compute distribution comparison metrics (Population Stability Index, Jensen-Shannon divergence, or equivalent) to compare current distributions to baseline.
- **Alert routing**: Drift exceeding the approved threshold generates an alert that is routed jointly to the model team and SecOps. The alert includes: which distribution drifted, magnitude, and a sample of recent inputs from the drifted segment. The joint routing ensures security teams can evaluate if drift is adversarial in nature; ML teams evaluate if it indicates natural data drift requiring retraining.
- **Drift + security correlation**: Every drift alert is automatically cross-correlated with concurrent SIEM events. Drift coinciding with adversarial input detection events is automatically elevated to high severity.

**Illustrative tooling**: Evidently AI, Arize, Fiddler, Whylogs (open source), or cloud-native ML monitoring (AWS Model Monitor, Azure ML monitoring) for drift computation; SIEM correlation rule for drift + adversarial event co-occurrence.

**NIST SP 800-53**: SI-4 (Information System Monitoring), CA-7 (Continuous Monitoring), NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.5

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-RAD-3.9.05.md#pattern-4-adversarial-input-and-model-extraction-detection]

### Pattern 4: Adversarial Input and Model Extraction Detection

**Purpose**: Detect active adversarial probing against production AI models — including systematic input perturbation (evasion), model extraction (querying to reconstruct model weights or decision boundary), and data poisoning via feedback loops.

**Design**:
- **Model-level query pattern monitoring**: The inference API telemetry stream feeds a behavioral analytics engine that tracks per-identity and per-source query patterns. Anomalies detected:
  - **Volume spike**: Queries from a single identity far exceeding baseline query rate (potential extraction or scraping)
  - **Perturbation pattern**: Sequential inputs with small systematic variations, consistent with adversarial example search
  - **Boundary probing pattern**: Distribution of prediction confidence values skewed toward decision boundaries (consistent with model extraction)
  - **Repeated near-threshold queries**: Same or very similar inputs repeated with minor variations (consistent with evading a threshold-based classifier)
- **Correlation with access logs**: Query pattern anomalies are correlated with authentication and access logs — unexpected sources, unusual times of access, or credential anomalies compound the risk score.
- **Adaptive throttling integration**: Detection outputs signal to the inference API rate limiter (owned by MODEL domain) that a specific identity should be throttled or blocked. The signal channel between OPS detection and MODEL enforcement is a documented interface between the two domains.

**Illustrative tooling**: Statistical analysis workloads running on the telemetry data lake (using Spark, Flink, or equivalent); custom detection functions in SIEM; SIEM-to-inference-API integration via API for adaptive throttling.

**NIST SP 800-53**: SI-4 (Information System Monitoring), SC-5 (Denial-of-Service Protection), NIST AI RMF MEASURE 4.1

### Pattern 5: AI Incident Response Playbooks

**Purpose**: Ensure consistent, documented, and practiced incident response for AI-specific security events, with clear escalation paths and evidence preservation guidance.

**Playbook library structure**:

Each AI system in production MUST have a designated playbook. Playbooks are created from the following templates:

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-RAD-3.9.05.md#template-1-adversarial-input--model-evasion-incident]

#### Template 1: Adversarial Input / Model Evasion Incident

| Step | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Acknowledge detection alert; assign incident ID | SecOps on-call |
| 2 | Throttle or block identified source IPs / identities at inference API | SecOps (via MODEL team coordination) |
| 3 | Preserve: raw query telemetry for incident period + prediction logs + source identity logs | SecOps |
| 4 | Notify ML team to evaluate model behavioral impact | SecOps → ML Team |
| 5 | ML Team: assess whether model was successfully evaded; quantify affected decisions if production decisions were impacted | ML Team |
| 6 | Evaluate whether decisions need to be reviewed or reversed; escalate to affected business unit | ML Team + Business Owner |
| 7 | Determine if retraining or model rollback is required | ML Team |
| 8 | Document root cause, affected scope, remediation actions | SecOps + ML Team |
| 9 | Update detection rules based on observed attack pattern | SecOps |
page_texts.16:
[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-RAD-3.9.05.md#template-2-model-extraction-incident]

#### Template 2: Model Extraction Incident

| Step | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Acknowledge detection alert; assign incident ID | SecOps on-call |
| 2 | Block identified source at API gateway and inference API | SecOps |
| 3 | Preserve: complete query logs for the actor's session history | SecOps |
| 4 | Assess whether enough queries were captured to represent significant IP theft risk | ML Team |
| 5 | Escalate to Legal if significant IP theft risk is assessed | ML Team + Legal |
| 6 | Evaluate access controls and authentication for how the source obtained API access | SecOps |
| 7 | Harden rate limiting and detection thresholds | SecOps + MODEL team |
| 8 | Document RCA and update detection playbook | SecOps |

[strategy/guidance/security/Artificial-Intelligence/ref-arch/GUID-SEC-AI-OPS-RAD-3.9.05.md#template-3-llm-prompt-injection--jailbreak-incident]

#### Template 3: LLM Prompt Injection / Jailbreak Incident

| Step | Action | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Acknowledge alert; assess severity based on what content was output | SecOps on-call |
| 2 | If PHI or sensitive data disclosed in output: invoke HIPAA breach assessment workflow | SecOps + GRC / Privacy Officer |
| 3 | Preserve: complete prompt and output logs for the incident session | SecOps |
| 4 | Block or shadow-ban the user account / session if attack is active | APP team |
| 5 | APP team: patch prompt construction to close identified injection vector | APP team |
| 6 | Test patch in staging environment; validate injection is no longer possible | APP team |
| 7 | Deploy patch; validate in production | APP team |
| 8 | Update SIEM detection rule for observed injection pattern | SecOps |
| 9 | If PHI breach confirmed: complete breach notification assessment per HIPAA timetable | GRC / Privacy Officer |

**NIST SP 800-53**: IR-4 (Incident Handling), IR-8 (Incident Response Plan), IR-9 (Information Spillage Response), AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information)

### Pattern 6: Explainability Record Store

**Purpose**: Produce and retain feature attribution explanations for high-stakes AI decisions to support audit, investigation, and minimum-necessary analysis.

**Design**:
- **Trigger conditions**: An explanation is automatically generated and stored for:
  - All decisions with a configurable high-impact classification (e.g., claim denials, authorization decisions, benefit eligibility determinations)
  - Any decision that is subsequently disputed or flagged for review
  - A random 1% sample of all other production decisions (configurable per model)
- **Explanation method**: The specific attribution method (SHAP, LIME, integrated gradients, attention visualization, or model-native explanation API) is selected per model based on the model type and operational latency constraints. SHAP is a common choice for tabular models; attention visualization for transformer models. The requirement is that attributions are mathematically meaningful and reproducible.
- **Storage schema**: Each explanation record includes: decision ID (cross-reference to the interaction log), model version, input feature values (data-classification-permitting), top N contributing features with direction and magnitude, explanation method used, and generation timestamp.
- **Retention**: Explanation records are retained consistent with the data classification of the underlying decision (minimum the retention schedule of the associated decision artifact; minimum 6 years for HIPAA-covered decisions).

**Illustrative tooling**: Open-source explanation libraries (SHAP, Captum for PyTorch, InterpretML); enterprise model monitoring platforms that provide built-in explanation logging (Fiddler, Vertex AI Explainability, Azure ML Responsible AI).

**NIST SP 800-53**: AU-2 (Audit Events), AU-11 (Audit Record Retention), NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.6

### Monitoring Readiness Lifecycle

| Phase | Key Activities | NIST SP 800-53 |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-deployment | Determine AI threat model; define behavioral baseline data source; configure SIEM log sources; verify playbook exists | RA-3, SI-4, IR-8 |
| Baseline establishment | Ingest first-N inference records; compute behavioral distributions; set detection thresholds | CA-7, SI-4 |
| Initial production monitoring | Alert sensitivity calibration; false positive tuning; first drift threshold validation | CA-7, SI-4 |
| Steady-state operations | Continuous drift monitoring; ongoing SIEM rule execution; monthly threat intel refresh; incident response exercises | CA-7, IR-4, RA-3 |
| Model update / retraining | Re-establish behavioral baseline post-retraining; validate detection rules still apply to new version | CM-3, CA-7 |
| Model decommission | Archive monitoring data per retention schedule; close SIEM log sources for decommissioned workload | AU-11, CM-8 |
